analysis.one_liner: Bans doctors from referring patients to imaging, therapy, and equipment businesses they own, in any health plan.
analysis.headline: The bill never got its own vote, but its self-referral ban was folded into the 1993 budget reconciliation bill (H.R. 2264), which passed and became the 'Stark II' law.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law already barred doctors from referring Medicare patients to clinical labs they had a financial stake in. This bill would extend that ban to every payer, not just Medicare, and cover five more services: lab work, physical therapy, imaging and radiology, radiation therapy, and medical equipment like wheelchairs. A doctor could no longer send you to an X-ray shop or therapy clinic he partially owned and profit from your visit.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and the programs and insurers that pay their bills. When a doctor profits from ordering a scan, therapy session, or piece of equipment, more of those services get ordered and billed. The bill would cut that incentive across Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurance, lowering costs and reducing care driven by ownership rather than medical need [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Extends the self-referral ban to all payors — Medicare, Medicaid, other federal and state health programs, and private insurance — by changing 'for which payment may be made under this title' to any service 'for which a charge is imposed' [S2][S3].

Adds physical therapy, radiology and diagnostic imaging, radiation therapy, and durable medical equipment to the services covered by the ban, on top of the clinical lab services already restricted [S2][S3].
Makes payment denial explicit for any claim presented in violation of the ban, so neither the patient nor the insurer can be billed for a self-referred service [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Physicians and companies that own or invest in imaging centers, physical therapy and radiation therapy clinics, and durable medical equipment suppliers. They would lose the ability to route their own patients to businesses they profit from, and existing ownership arrangements would have two years to unwind [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Doctor-owned imaging, therapy, and equipment businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill preserves a broad exception for HMOs and managed care plans, including any plan where physicians bear 'significant financial risk' for service costs — so self-referral and financial incentives stay legal inside managed care, the fastest-growing part of the market [S3].
It adds a waiver letting the Secretary exempt arrangements that provide 'necessary, valuable community services,' a discretion that could preserve some ownership deals [S3].

A good-faith objection: in rural or underserved areas, a doctor's ownership stake is sometimes the only reason an imaging or therapy service exists there at all, and the ban could shut those services down or push physicians to stop offering them.
The two-year effective date for pre-existing financial relationships gives established doctor-owned ventures a long runway to keep operating under the old rules [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — extending the anti-kickback-style self-referral ban beyond Medicare labs to imaging, therapy, and equipment across all payers — targets a well-documented driver of unnecessary care and cost, and it is the expansion Congress ultimately wrote into law as 'Stark II.' The design flaws are real: the managed-care carve-out and the community-services waiver leave sizable loopholes, and the long transition protects incumbents. On balance a consumer-protective bill, weakened at the edges but sound at the core.

outcome.mechanism: The bill never got a vote in the House or Senate on its own; the record's final entry points its substance to H.R. 2264, and its provisions were enacted through that budget reconciliation bill as the 'Stark II' law.

narrative.text: Rep. John Kasich introduced the bill on February 2, 1993, with Rep. Rick Santorum as its one cosponsor [S1][S4].
It was referred jointly to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees, then to their health subcommittees, where it sat for six months [S5].

The action history's final entry, dated August 10, 1993, is a pointer to H.R. 2264 — the budget reconciliation bill for that Congress — indicating the bill's provisions were carried into that measure rather than advanced separately [S5].

The extension of the self-referral ban to Medicaid and to physical therapy, imaging, radiation therapy, and durable medical equipment became law in that reconciliation act, known in health policy as the 'Stark II' law, effective in 1995 with the same two-year transition for existing financial relationships.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients and Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers came out ahead: the ban they wanted was enacted through the reconciliation bill. Physician owners of imaging centers, therapy clinics, and equipment businesses lost a profitable referral channel.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients and insurers; doctor-owned facilities lost

for.name: Rep. John Kasich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to extend the self-referral ban to all payors and additional services.

for.name: Rep. Rick Santorum
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Held the bill for six months in their health subcommittees without a markup or vote, after which its substance was directed to the reconciliation bill instead.

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsor and cosponsor were Republicans, but physician self-referral restrictions drew support across party lines in this era, and no recorded vote or party bloc opposed the bill itself.

industries.industry: Physician-owned imaging, physical therapy, radiation therapy, and medical equipment businesses
industries.note: These ventures exist because a referring doctor profits from sending patients to a facility he owns, which tends to increase the volume of scans, therapy, and equipment billed to patients and insurers. The bill would cut off that revenue stream for existing and new ownership arrangements, with a two-year phase-out for deals already in place.

The bill rewrites the exception so HMOs and managed care plans — including any plan where doctors bear significant financial risk for service costs — can continue arrangements that would otherwise violate the ban. That locks in self-referral inside prepaid plans even as it shuts it down elsewhere.

The bill loosens one hospital exception, requiring only a Medicare participation agreement, while the broader ban on physician ownership of competing imaging and therapy services reduces competition to hospital departments for these services.
